setting.tex: If the alphabet that defines these sentences is finite (e.g., the finite English alphabet \{a,b,...,z\}), and sentences themselves are finite, then a language may further be thought of as a countable subset of a countable universe $U$ of all possible strings.
Let $\cD$ be an unknown distribution over the universe $U$, and let $\supp(\cD)$ denote its support (i.e., elements of $U$ that have positive mass under $\cD$).

\[

quotes.tex:
Let $ \cC$ be a countable collection and $\cD$ be a distribution over the universe $U$. If $ i(\cC,\cD) < \infty $, and there exists a language $ L\in \cC$ such that $ L\subseteq \supp(\cD) $,
    then with probability at least $1-c\cdot\exp(-C\cdot n)$ over $ \rS\sim \cD^{n} $ (where $c, C$ are constants depending only on $U, \cD $ and $ \cC$,
    the string $\cA(\rS)$ returned by \Cref{alg:generation} satisfies $\cA(\rS) \in \supp(\cD) \setminus \rS$. Namely,
    $
       \generr(\cA, \cD, n)\leq c\cdot\exp(-C\cdot n).
    $

There exists a countable universe $U$, a enummeration of this universe, and a countable language collection $\cC\subseteq 2^U$ such that the following holds. For every deterministic generation algorithm $\bar{\cA}$, there exists a distribution
$\cD\in  \bar{\cP}_{gen}(\cC)
 =
 \{\cD\in \cP(U): \exists L\in \cC,\ L\subseteq \supp(\cD),\ i(\cD,\cC)=\infty \}$ such that
\begin{align*}
    \limsup_{n\to\infty}\generr(\bar{\cA},\cD,n)\geq \frac{1}{2}.
\end{align*}
